learn.title: Green ammonia: clean fuel for shipping and fertilisers
learn.intro: Green ammonia is a clean fuel that can power ships and fertiliser plants without carbon emissions, offering a pathway to decarbonise global shipping and agriculture while supporting energy security.
learn.c1_text: Green ammonia is made by splitting water into hydrogen and nitrogen using renewable electricity. For example, the world's largest green ammonia plant in Australia can produce 1,000 tonnes of ammonia per year. This fuel can power cargo ships and fertiliser factories, replacing diesel and fossil fuels.
learn.c2_text: The process uses electrolysers powered by solar or wind to split water into hydrogen and nitrogen. The hydrogen is then mixed with nitrogen to form ammonia. This method is scalable and can be used in ports, shipping hubs, and large industrial sites to reduce emissions.
learn.c3_text: India is building its green ammonia capacity. The National Green Hydrogen Mission targets 5 million tonnes of green hydrogen production by 2030. Indian refineries and fertiliser plants are exploring green ammonia to cut emissions and reduce import dependence on fossil fuels.
learn.stat1: Global green ammonia capacity expected to reach 10 million tonnes by 2030 (IRENA, 2022)
learn.stat2: Australia's largest green ammonia plant produces 1,000 tonnes per year (IRENA, 2022)
learn.stat3: India's National Green Hydrogen Mission targets 5 million tonnes of green hydrogen production by 2030
learn.stat4: The shipping sector accounts for about 3% of global CO2 emissions, making green ammonia a key decarbonisation tool (IRENA, 2022)

learn.title: Concentrated Solar Power: using mirrors to generate electricity
learn.intro: Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) uses mirrors to focus sunlight onto a receiver, generating heat that drives turbines to produce electricity. This technology is ideal for large-scale solar projects and can store heat for later use.
learn.c1_text: Concentrated Solar Power uses large mirrors to focus sunlight onto a receiver, heating a fluid that drives a turbine to generate electricity. A typical CSP plant uses 10,000 mirrors to concentrate sunlight onto a single receiver, producing up to 50 MW of electricity.
learn.c2_title: 🏗️ How does the mirror system work?
learn.c2_text: The mirrors, often called parabolic troughs or solar power towers, focus sunlight onto a receiver tube. The concentrated heat boils a working fluid like molten salt, which stores thermal energy. This stored heat can then power a steam turbine to generate electricity even after sunset.
learn.c3_text: India's Kamuthi CSP plant in Tamil Nadu is one of the world's largest, generating 620 MW. India's solar policy supports CSP as a dispatchable renewable source, with the National Solar Mission targeting 40 GW of solar capacity by 2030.
learn.stat1: Kamuthi CSP plant in Tamil Nadu generates 620 MW (IRENA, 2022)
learn.stat2: India's National Solar Mission targets 40 GW of solar capacity by 2030
learn.stat3: CSP plants can store heat for up to 6 hours, providing dispatchable electricity (IRENA, 2022)
learn.stat4: A single CSP plant can replace 100,000 tonnes of CO2 emissions annually (IRENA, 2022)

learn.title: Electric buses and trucks: commercial vehicle electrification explained
learn.intro: Electric buses and trucks are replacing diesel vehicles in urban and long-haul transport, reducing emissions and operating costs. This shift is accelerating as battery costs fall and charging infrastructure expands.
learn.c1_text: Electric buses and trucks reduce tailpipe emissions and operating costs. For example, a 100-metre bus route can save 1,000 tonnes of CO2 per year. Electric trucks can haul heavy loads for 200 km on a single charge, making them ideal for short-to-medium haulage.
learn.c2_text: Electric buses and trucks use onboard batteries that are charged via grid electricity or renewable sources. Charging can be done overnight at depots or during rest periods. The charging time depends on battery size, with fast chargers capable of adding 80% charge in under 30 minutes.
learn.c3_text: India's FAME II scheme offers incentives for electric buses and trucks. The National Electric Mobility Mission aims for 30% electric two-wheelers and 10% electric three-wheelers by 2030. Indian cities like Delhi and Mumbai are leading the adoption of electric buses.
learn.stat1: Electric buses save 1,000 tonnes of CO2 per year per 100 km route (IRENA, 2023)
learn.stat2: Fast chargers can add 80% charge in under 30 minutes (IRENA, 2023)
learn.stat3: India's FAME II scheme provides incentives for electric buses and trucks
learn.stat4: India aims for 30% electric two-wheelers and 10% electric three-wheelers by 2030 (IRENA, 2023)

learn.title: Capacity factor explained: why rated power differs from actual output
learn.intro: Capacity factor is the ratio of actual energy produced to the maximum possible energy. It explains why a power plant rated at 500 MW might only produce 200 MW on average.
learn.c1_text: Capacity factor measures how much of a plant's maximum power it actually produces over time. A 500 MW plant with a 50% capacity factor produces 250 MW on average. This is the difference between theoretical maximum and real-world performance.
learn.c2_text: Capacity factor depends on weather, downtime, and maintenance. A solar plant with a 20% capacity factor produces 20% of its rated power. A wind farm with a 35% capacity factor produces 35% of its rated power. These factors reflect the intermittent nature of renewables.
learn.c3_text: India's solar capacity factor averages 17-22%. Wind capacity factors range from 25-35%. India's grid has seen capacity factors improve with better forecasting and storage. The National Solar Mission aims to increase the capacity factor through better grid management.
learn.stat2: Wind capacity factors range from 25-35% in India (EIA, 2023)
learn.stat3: A 500 MW plant with 50% capacity factor produces 250 MW on average (EIA, 2023)
learn.stat4: India's grid has improved capacity factors with better forecasting and storage (EIA, 2023)

learn.title: How the electricity grid balances supply and demand in real time
learn.intro: The electricity grid must balance supply and demand every second. This is achieved through a mix of generation, storage, and demand response, ensuring stable and reliable electricity for all consumers.
learn.c1_text: The grid balances supply and demand in real time by adjusting generation to match consumption. When demand exceeds supply, frequency drops, triggering protective measures. When supply exceeds demand, frequency rises, requiring output reduction. This continuous balancing is the backbone of grid stability.
learn.c2_text: Grid operators use demand response, storage, and flexible generation. Battery storage can absorb excess power during high production and release it during high demand. The grid also uses predictive algorithms to anticipate demand and adjust generation accordingly, ensuring a stable 50/60 Hz frequency.
learn.c3_text: India's grid management has improved with better forecasting and renewable integration. The National Grid Code requires utilities to maintain frequency within a range. India's renewable integration mandates require grid operators to balance supply and demand as renewables increase.
learn.stat1: Grid frequency is maintained at 50/60 Hz in India (US Dept of Energy, 2023)
learn.stat2: Battery storage can absorb excess power and release it during peak demand (US Dept of Energy, 2023)
learn.stat3: India's renewable integration mandates require grid operators to balance supply and demand (US Dept of Energy, 2023)
learn.stat4: Predictive algorithms help grid operators anticipate demand and adjust generation (US Dept of Energy, 2023)

learn.title: How solar PV panels generate electricity using the photoelectric effect
learn.intro: Solar PV panels convert sunlight into electricity using the photoelectric effect, where photons from sunlight knock electrons loose from silicon atoms, creating an electric current.
learn.c1_text: Solar PV panels use the photoelectric effect to convert sunlight into electricity. When photons from sunlight hit the silicon cells, they knock electrons loose, creating a flow of electrons. This current is then captured and converted into usable electricity.
learn.c2_text: Photons from sunlight hit the semiconductor material in PV cells, knocking electrons free. This creates an electric current. Silicon, the main material, has a band gap that allows electrons to move freely, generating a voltage. A typical 1 m² panel produces about 1 kW of electricity.
learn.c3_text: India has installed over 60 GW of solar PV capacity. The Indian government's PLI scheme for solar manufacturing aims to make solar panels domestically. The National Solar Mission targets 100 GW of solar capacity by 2030, with rooftop and utility-scale projects driving growth.

learn.stat3: India's PLI scheme for solar manufacturing aims to make panels domestically (US Dept of Energy, 2023)
